title: Stan Kenton, Balboa Beach and playing like Earl Hines
summary: Hazel tells of helping stranded musicians in California, seeing Kenton on piano, and challenging him about sounding like Hines.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Later, he got more frenzied as he got into another kind of music. Well, you changed like that. I've seen bands do that. I've seen bands make a national reputation playing one style. And the minute they get in the money, they changed the band around and play all together different. And it synced. Kenton is one that did that. He got more wild and more wild as he was. There's a funny thing about Kenton. I was out in California in 1934 to 1938 with Gene Austin. And I went down to Balboa Beach. And there had a bunch of boys in a band down there. A fella by the name of Hank Halstead had the band down there. And a bunch of the boys had been in a band called Ray Millers that he had left stranded here. He played at the Roosevelt. And he left them stranded here. And four or five of the boys, Vito Musa was one of them. Sammy Taylor was the drummer. He wound up with Phil Harris. And four or five of them. A fella by the name of Charlie DuPont and I kind of helped them out a little bit until they could get some money from California to get back home, you know. And they invited me to come down to Balboa and hear the band. And they were playing in a big ballroom. So they get this big, great big band, maybe 18 men. And Kenton's playing piano in this band, you see. And then a few years later on, he gets this progressive band. And he comes in the family store one night. And I got to talk to him. And I'd ask him, I said, now what I want to know is this. I've been listening to all this artistry and rhythm and all this business that you put in on. But what I want to know is every time it gets to time for you to play, you play like Father Hines. How come you do that? And he did.
He just left. He said, well.
He changed the way I play.

And I don't think he ever changed. The last time I heard the band, he was still playing like Father Hines. Because that was his idol. Father Hines in those days was his idol, you know. And I thought that's so funny. He's got all this progressive music around. I think at that time he had Ferguson and all that bunch of guys. Rosalini and all that. Paul Desmond, I think, at the time, was with him too. Cooper. Bunch of guys. That's Shelley Mann. Every time it comes to... What do you think of Shelley Mann? I like Shelley very much. I like the things he's doing. He's way over my head. I didn't study much. stuff
